summary: The manuscript argues that a small labelled pilot determines a ridge calibration's learning curve only above an 'observability horizon'. It proposes a prior-free identification set and an information fraction to show this limit, plus a Bayesian regularisation-path matching forecaster (B-RPM) with a structural prior on alignment and noise, evaluated on 38 public NIR/MIR/VisNIR tasks. The theoretical point is valuable and well supported: pilot-only extrapolation must import prior information, and power-law extrapolation from small pilots is optimistic. The paper is transparent about its design history. As a practical planning paper for ACA, however, it does not yet deliver. The pre-specified hypotheses HB1-HB3 failed. On level error the no-improvement rule remains the best forecaster. No method beats the base rate on the one evaluated decision, and the identification set is almost never narrow enough to decide anything. The recommended staged design is never tested. The headline 'least biased' claim comes from soil (optimistic) and mixture/fuel (pessimistic) biases cancelling: mean absolute task-level bias is 0.170 for B-RPM against 0.175 for FLAT. Evaluation is against ridge on sub-sampled spectra rather than PLS. The reference-error floor, which the paper itself identifies as the main driver of slope, is not used as the prior information labs actually have. The robustness section has text-table inconsistencies and selective summaries. The text is long and statistically dense for ACA's readership.
strengths: Clear and useful negative result: Proposition 1 formalises why pilot-only learning-curve extrapolation cannot determine the future gain. This explains the familiar optimism of power-law extrapolation and the strength of the no-improvement rule.

The deterministic-equivalent theory reproduces ridge and PLS learning curves across 38 tasks (MALE 0.130/0.153), and the κ-collapse test (SD 0.037 vs 0.515) is a convincing check of the structural assumption.

The interpretation of the alignment exponent (r<1 everywhere; lower for VisNIR/SWNIR than for MIR) and of the noise floor as the main slope determinant is chemically meaningful and new to this literature.

Careful leakage control: replicate averaging, site- or profile-level groups, exact leave-one-group-out CV, and unlabelled spectra taken from the pool only. Task- and source-level statistics with Holm correction.
Failed hypotheses are reported in the body and the Limitations, and post-hoc analyses are labelled as such. Code is fully reproducible from a single script.

Transferring structural parameters instead of empirical slopes is a sound idea. The cross-family level-error result (B-RPM-LOFO 0.292 vs SLOPE-T-LOFO 0.392) shows a real advantage over transferring curves.

issues.title: 'Least biased forecaster' is an artefact of cross-family cancellation
issues.description: The headline claim (abstract, Sec. 4.4, conclusions) that B-RPM is the least biased forecaster (mean bias +0.008, within +/-0.040 up to 8x) rests on averaging signed task-level biases of opposite sign across families. Per family B-RPM is systematically biased. Soil (23 of 38 tasks) is consistently optimistic by about 8% RMSEP at every horizon. Designed mixtures are strongly pessimistic, and fuel becomes pessimistic at 8x. If you average the magnitude of each task's bias instead, B-RPM is no better than the no-improvement rule. For an analyst the relevant quantity is the bias on their own task, not the benchmark average.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from results/raw/forecasts_bayes_*.csv and forecasts_main_*.csv (ratio>=2). Mean task-level signed bias: B-RPM +0.008, FLAT +0.139. Mean |task-level bias|: B-RPM 0.170, FLAT 0.175, RPM 0.183, IPL3 0.269. B-RPM bias by family and ratio: soil -0.083/-0.075/-0.079/-0.094/-0.083 at 2/4/8/16/32x; mixture +0.447/+0.799 at 2/4x; fuel +0.025/+0.071/+0.185 at 2/4/8x; pharma -0.172 at 8x and -0.312 at 16x; fruit -0.199 at 32x. Fig. 5 (Mango, n0=50): the B-RPM forecast at n=1600 is about 0.68 against a truth of about 1.05.
issues.corrective_action: Report the mean absolute task-level bias and the per-family bias by horizon (a new column in Table 2 and a panel in Fig. 7). Rephrase the abstract, highlights and conclusions: B-RPM's biases cancel across families in the benchmark aggregate, but on individual tasks they are as large as those of FLAT. Discuss the systematic optimism for soil, where most real users would apply the method.

issues.title: The planning workflow (extend / stop / second batch) is not shown to support any decision
issues.description: Fig. 1 and Sec. 4.8 present a decision workflow, but the decision-level results are negative or missing. (a) On the only decision that was evaluated ('8x more samples reduce RMSEP by >=15%'), no method beat the base rate, and B-RPM was worse than FLAT. (b) The identification set is almost never narrow enough to inform a decision, so recommendation (ii) reduces to 'always collect a second batch'. That is generic advice and needs none of the machinery. (c) The staged design recommended in the conclusions was never evaluated: the paper does not show how much a second batch narrows the forecast, or what a sequential rule saves in reference analyses. (d) B-RPM was not evaluated on the pre-registered sample-size-for-target metric (Table S29 covers RPM, IPL and FLAT but not B-RPM), which is the question a lab actually asks: how many samples do I need to reach X? (e) There is no cost model or decision-relevant threshold. The 15%-at-8x threshold is arbitrary and is not tied to required RMSEP, RPD or a specification limit. A lab reading the paper would end up running a pilot, then running a second batch, as it would have done anyway.
issues.evidence: TB6: Brier B-RPM 0.290, FLAT 0.274, IPL3 0.277, climatology 0.247. From the raw forecasts, the share of pilots whose identification set spans less than a factor 1.5 in RMSEP is 3.2% at n/n0=2, 2.8% at 4x and 1.9% at 8x. Median width factor: 3.4 at 2x, 15 at 8x, 58 at >=32x (TB5). Table S29 and T6_sample_size_decisions.csv contain no B-RPM rows. Sec. 6 recommends a staged design, but no staged experiment is reported.
issues.corrective_action: Either demonstrate decision value or reframe the contribution as diagnostic, i.e. why pilot-only planning cannot work, and not as a planning tool. Add B-RPM to the n-for-target metric. Specify the workflow as an explicit algorithm: inputs, thresholds and the decision rule, expressed in units the analyst uses (target RMSEP or RPD, cost per reference analysis). Evaluate that algorithm.
issues.proposed_experiment: A retrospective staged-design simulation on the existing 38 tasks (computational only). Stage 1: a pilot of n0 in {50,100}. Stage 2: add a second batch of n0 and refit B-RPM (or a two-point learning curve) using both batches. Decision: whether the target RMSEP (for example the RMSEP truly achieved at 8 n0, or a target expressed as RPD) is reachable within the budget, and the n required. Compare against fixed designs (n0 only; a full budget up front; ASTM E1655-style rules) on the number of reference analyses spent, the probability of meeting the target, and regret. Report the n-for-target error for B-RPM as in Table S29.

issues.title: Abstract and conclusions select favourable endpoints and omit the failed pre-specified hypotheses
issues.description: The primary pre-specified hypothesis HB1 (B-RPM-LOFO has a lower gain error than SLOPE-T-LOFO) failed. Instead, the abstract reports the post-hoc level-endpoint comparison (0.292 vs 0.392, p=0.001) as evidence that B-RPM 'kept its accuracy'. HB2 (non-inferiority to FLAT) and HB3 (band calibration) also failed. None of the three failures appears in the abstract, the Significance statement or the conclusions; they appear only in the Limitations. Other results are not mentioned in the text: under LOFO, B-RPM is significantly worse than FLAT on the level endpoint, and on the gain endpoint the unlabelled-spectrum scaling estimator WEI is nominally better than B-RPM.
issues.evidence: TB2: HB1 gain +0.006, p=0.72. HB2 level -0.020 (CI -0.038 to -0.003), so non-inferiority was not met. B-RPM-LOFO vs FLAT on level: -0.030, CI -0.046 to -0.014, Holm p=0.008, B-RPM better on only 10/38 tasks. TB1 gain error: WEI 0.240 vs B-RPM 0.265 (p=0.98), SLOPE-T 0.188. TB4: raw 80% bands cover 55%.
issues.corrective_action: State in the abstract that FLAT remained the most accurate level forecaster, that HB1-HB3 were not met, and that the cross-family comparison on the primary (gain) endpoint showed no difference. Label the level-endpoint LOFO comparison as secondary. Mention the WEI gain result in Sec. 4.4.

issues.title: Ridge ground truth on sub-sampled spectra does not match calibration practice (PLS, full resolution)
issues.description: All B-RPM forecasts are scored against the ridge ground truth. Practitioners calibrate with PLS and choose the number of latent variables by CV, at full spectral resolution and often with derivatives. The theory reproduces PLS curves (MALE 0.153), but B-RPM is never scored against the PLS truth: Table S20 and T4 contain only the version-1 methods. The 100-220-variable wavelength sub-sampling is not described (decimation or binning? before or after smoothing?). The eigen-spectrum, p/n, the horizon κ0 and therefore the whole observability argument depend on that choice. SNV is applied after sub-sampling, which changes the SNV statistics. Mango has p=94, which contradicts the stated range of 100-220.
issues.evidence: Sec. 3.2; Table S20 / T4_main_accuracy_pls_truth.csv (no B-RPM rows); T1_tasks.csv (Mango p=94).
issues.corrective_action: Score B-RPM and the main comparators against the PLS ground truth, and add the result to Table 2. Document the sub-sampling (method, step, order relative to SNV). Run a sensitivity analysis at full or less-decimated resolution on a few tasks. Discuss whether the prior (r, η) depends on preprocessing and resolution, and if it does, provide priors per preprocessing.
issues.proposed_experiment: Rerun B-RPM, FLAT, IPL3 and SLOPE-T on the existing pilots, scored against the stored PLS truth (truth_pls_logrmse). On six representative tasks, compare 2x decimation against the current sub-sampling and report the change in eigen-decay, the alignment exponent r and forecast error.

issues.title: The reference-method error floor is not used explicitly, and B-RPM is weakest when reference noise increases
issues.description: Sec. 4.2 itself identifies the irreducible-noise fraction η as the main determinant of learning-curve slope. η combines reference-method error, sub-sampling and heterogeneity error (important for soils and intact fruit), spectral noise and non-linearity. In practice the reference-method component is often known: repeatability and reproducibility from ring tests, ISO/ASTM methods, or duplicate analyses that labs run routinely. That is exactly the prior information Proposition 1 says is needed, but the method draws its η prior from other materials instead. When reference noise was added, B-RPM was worse than FLAT (0.143 vs 0.117), and worse on 4 of 6 tasks. Most of the ACA chemometrics literature on how reference error limits apparent RMSEP is not discussed: RMSEP corrected for reference error, the reference-error floor, and figures of merit.
issues.evidence: T8 / robustness_raw.csv (ratio>=2), ref_noise: B-RPM 0.143, FLAT 0.117. Per task: KSSL-VisNIR:clay 0.161 vs 0.092, Tablets 0.149 vs 0.096, Neospectra pH 0.137 vs 0.107. RPM-TP (transferred lower bound) exists but is not developed.
issues.corrective_action: Add an option for a user-supplied reference-error variance σ_ref² as a hard or soft lower bound on η, together with guidance on obtaining it from duplicates. Report the apparent and the reference-corrected RMSEP floor. Relate the learning-curve plateau to the reference-error floor (e.g. DiFoggio; Faber & Kowalski) and to RPD/RER.
issues.proposed_experiment: On the ref_noise variant and on tasks with known reference repeatability (e.g. KSSL OC, tablets assay, Tecator), give B-RPM the added (known) noise variance as a lower bound on η. Compare its accuracy and calibration with the transferred-prior version and with FLAT.

issues.title: The robustness section has text-table inconsistencies, is selectively summarised and is underpowered
issues.description: (a) The numbers in Sec. 4.7 (computed at ratio>=2) do not match Table S33 / T8_robustness.csv, which include ratio=1 rows. (b) The text says B-RPM was less accurate than FLAT 'in these scenarios'. In fact B-RPM beat FLAT with Kennard-Stone pilots and under the orchard-population shift. The text also omits that the pre-registered RPM (r=1) was by far the most accurate method under the season shift. (c) The experiment is small: 6 tasks, n0 in {50,100}, 10 pilots, one split, and a single task (mango) for both shift scenarios. Results vary strongly between tasks, e.g. Mango raw spectra 0.338 vs 0.155 for FLAT, and Tablets with KS pilots 0.351 vs 0.158. (d) The B-RPM prior was learned from SNV fits and then applied to raw and SG1 spectra, so part of the loss may be a prior-preprocessing mismatch. This is not discussed. (e) Even on the i.i.d. mango seasons 1-3 split, B-RPM was worse than FLAT (0.212 vs 0.157).
issues.evidence: Text: FLAT raw 0.215, SG1 0.272; KS bias B-RPM +0.084, FLAT +0.233. T8/S33: FLAT raw 0.249, SG1 0.293; KS bias +0.118 and +0.250. Recomputed at ratio>=2: KS B-RPM 0.288 vs FLAT 0.298; population shift 0.182 vs 0.195; season shift RPM 0.086, RPM-T 0.105, B-RPM 0.503, FLAT 0.255.
issues.corrective_action: Make Table S33 and the text use the same horizon filter. Report all scenarios evenly, including those B-RPM wins and the RPM season result. Add per-task results. Relearn the prior for each preprocessing, or state that it was not relearned. Extend to more tasks and to n0=25 and 200, or tone down the general statements.
issues.proposed_experiment: Repeat the raw, SG1 and ref-noise variants on at least 12 tasks covering all families, with priors relearned on the matching preprocessing (LOSO), using n0 in {25,50,100,200} and the same pilot counts as the main study.

issues.title: 'Draw pilots at random' conflicts with practice, and the season-shift failure is not addressed
issues.description: Labs seldom draw calibration samples at random. They select spectrally (Kennard-Stone, Duplex, Puchwein, D-optimal) or stratify over known sources of variation (season, cultivar, site, instrument, batch). For agricultural products, future seasons cannot be sampled at all. B-RPM's worst failure was the realistic mango season shift (bias -0.502, twice that of FLAT). The recommendation 'draw pilots at random from the target population' therefore gives no practical guidance and partly contradicts established design practice. The paper also gives no advice on how to plan when the deployment population drifts.
issues.evidence: Sec. 4.7, T8: shift_season B-RPM bias -0.502, FLAT -0.255. ks_pilot: B-RPM bias +0.084. Anderson et al. [36] was built precisely to test season robustness.
issues.corrective_action: Discuss stratified and spectrally designed pilots. Propose a correction for KS pilots (e.g. weighting by spectral leverage) or report how far forecasts are inflated. For seasonal products, recommend a pilot stratified over the seasons available and a prior or variance component for between-season shift. State plainly that B-RPM predicts within-population gains only.
issues.proposed_experiment: Mango: pilots stratified over seasons 1-3 (and a leave-one-season-out variant of the pilot CV), with a between-season variance term estimated from the pilot added to the predictive distribution. Evaluate the season-4 forecast against FLAT and B-RPM as currently specified.

issues.title: Small and designed data sets support only short horizons; long-horizon and cross-family claims rest mainly on soil
issues.description: CGL and Tecator have a maximum truth size of n=100, so they enter only with n0=25 and 50 at ratios of 2-4. Diesel reaches 200 and Tablets 400. At ratio>=8 the evaluation contains 23 soil tasks, 6 fuel tasks (8x only), one fruit and one pharma task. So the claim 'within +/-0.040 up to eightfold' and the cross-family transfer result are in effect a soil-versus-rest comparison. For soil, the cross-family prior comes from 15 small, heterogeneous tasks. The designed CGL mixtures break the random-sampling premise (theory error 0.35-0.40, raw band coverage 11%, B-RPM bias +0.45/+0.80). For designed mixtures, sample-size planning is a design-of-experiments question (number and placement of design points), not a learning-curve question. 'Six application families' therefore overstates how general the evidence is.
issues.evidence: T1_tasks.csv max_n_truth: CGL/Tecator 100, Diesel 200, Tablets 400. Tasks with ratio>=8 by family: soil 23, fuel 6, fruit 1, pharma 1. TB4: mixture cov80 0.107. TB3: mixture level 0.569 vs FLAT 0.474.
issues.corrective_action: Give a table showing which families contribute at each extrapolation ratio. Report the main results with CGL excluded, or treat designed mixtures separately with an explicit statement that the method does not apply to them. Qualify the claims about generality across families.

issues.title: The information fraction is confounded with pilot size, can be negative, and its per-pilot warning value is overstated
issues.description: The tertile analysis (Table S12) pools pilot sizes, so 'low' tertiles are mostly n0=25 and 'high' tertiles mostly n0=100-200. Forecast error falls with n0 for every method, FLAT included. Within a pilot size, the fraction separates good from bad forecasts only modestly at n0=25-50 and not at all at n0=100-200, so the claimed 'per-pilot warning' is mostly a restatement of pilot size. The median information fraction in the low tertile is negative (-0.052), meaning posterior variance exceeds prior variance (prior-data conflict). That makes it not a fraction, and its interpretation is undefined. Recommendation (iii), 'at least 100 samples', comes from the model's own posterior and is not validated externally against decisions.
issues.evidence: Recomputed within n0 (B-RPM |log error| by low/mid/high tertile): n0=25 0.42/0.38/0.31; n0=50 0.33/0.28/0.22; n0=100 0.23/0.16/0.19; n0=200 0.14/0.14/0.13. TB7 low-tertile info median -0.052. Table S15: FLAT level error 0.326 at n0=25 and 0.182 at n0=100.
issues.corrective_action: Report the reliability of the information fraction within each pilot size. Define how negative values are handled and flag prior-data conflict explicitly, which may itself be the more useful warning. Support the >=100-sample recommendation with the decision-level analysis requested in R3-02.

issues.title: Readability for ACA's chemist readership; length and density
issues.description: The manuscript runs to about 10,300 words, with 43 supplementary tables and 17 forecaster variants. Sec. 2 is written for statisticians: deterministic equivalents, the effective penalty κ, df2, the proposition with its proof, partial identification. Many coined terms are layered on top of each other: observability horizon, identification set, information fraction, alignment exponent, B-RPM-LOFO/-r/-0/-m10, RPM-T/TD/TP/w. Results are reported in log-ratio units that most chemists do not translate into % RMSEP. Nowhere is the abstract theory connected to spectroscopic intuition, e.g. minor constituents whose bands overlap strongly carry signal in low-variance principal components, and these components only become learnable at larger n. That is essentially what r<1 means, and it relates to net analyte signal.
issues.evidence: Secs 2.2-2.5; Table 2 lists 13 methods; Table S6 lists 17. Equations come out garbled in the text version.
issues.corrective_action: Move the proof and the RPM-w details to the SI. Add a one-paragraph chemical interpretation of κ0 and r, using principal components and net analyte signal. Add a worked example with real numbers (one pilot of 50 mango or soil samples: forecast, identification set, information fraction, decision). Cut the main-text comparators to about 5 (B-RPM, FLAT, IPL3, SLOPE-T, RPM). State errors as % RMSEP (0.10 log is about 10%). Aim for about 7,000 words.

issues.title: Missing comparisons and references that a chemometrics referee would expect
issues.description: (a) Riley et al. and Konstantinidis et al. are cited but never compared numerically. Compute their minimum n for these tasks, using the R² estimated from the pilot and an effective number of parameters (e.g. PLS LVs or df), and compare with the learning-curve results. (b) Standard sample-number guidance (ASTM E1655, ISO 12099, Naes et al. 'User-friendly guide') is not cited or used as a baseline. (c) Net analyte signal and figures of merit (sensitivity, selectivity, LOD; Lorber et al.; Olivieri's reviews), which tie analyte signal in low-variance directions to achievable error, are absent. (d) The literature on reference-error effects on RMSEP is missing (DiFoggio 1995; Faber & Kowalski 1997). (e) Esbensen & Geladi on validation is missing. (f) For soil, the realistic alternative to a new pilot is a large library with memory-based learning or spiking with local samples (Ramirez-Lopez et al.; Guerrero et al.). The Limitations mention local methods but not this planning scenario. (g) Beleites et al. 2013 is cited only for test-set size, but its learning-curve approach to sample-size planning is the closest chemometric precedent and should be discussed properly. Riley et al. 2019 (continuous outcomes, Stat Med) is the more relevant Riley paper.
issues.corrective_action: Add these references. Add Riley/Konstantinidis and an ASTM/ISO rule-of-thumb as baselines in the n-for-target analysis. Discuss the NAS and figure-of-merit interpretation and library/spiking planning scenarios.
issues.proposed_experiment: For each task and pilot, compute the Riley/Konstantinidis minimum n (shrinkage >=0.9, small optimism) from the pilot R² and effective df, plus the ASTM E1655 minimum, and compare them with the n truly needed to reach the RMSEP attained at 4 n0 and 16 n0.

issues.title: Transformed-unit RMSEP and lack of analyst-facing figures of merit
issues.description: OC and CEC are modelled as log(1+y). The forecasts and Fig. 5 show RMSEP in transformed or unlabelled units, while labs report RMSEP in original units, together with RPD/RPIQ or relative error against a specification.
issues.evidence: Sec. 3.1; Fig. 5 y-axis has no units.
issues.corrective_action: Label units. Back-transform, or explain that transformed-scale RMSEP is used. Add RPD/RPIQ for the final calibrations so readers can judge whether a forecast gain matters.

issues.title: The pre-registration of B-RPM is weaker than presented
issues.description: B-RPM was designed in response to version-1 results on the same 38 tasks and the same pilots, and its priors are learned from the same benchmark (LOSO). Pre-specifying before version-2 outputs were inspected rules out tuning on outputs, but this is not a confirmatory test on new data. HB4 appears in the manuscript, but in Note 2 it is not listed as a separate hypothesis. Identification-set coverage at n/n0=2 (88%) is below the 90% target; this is not stated.
issues.corrective_action: Describe the study as pre-specified re-analysis of the same data, not as confirmatory. Report HB4 per horizon. Ideally, validate B-RPM on one or two NIR data sets held out from the whole development, e.g. another public fruit, grain or pharma set.
issues.proposed_experiment: Run B-RPM on 2-3 public NIR regression sets never used during development (e.g. the corn data, a wheat protein set, or the IDRC shoot-outs from other years), with the frozen code and prior.

issues.title: Data handling details missing for the non-soil sets
issues.description: The paper does not say which IDRC 2002 tablet instrument(s) were used, or whether the two instruments were averaged. Tecator N=215 differs from the usual 240 samples. Whether diesel samples have replicates or duplicate spectra is not described. The sub-sampling scheme is missing (see R3-04). Table 1 is incomplete in the text version (N, p and max n missing for the non-soil rows).
issues.corrective_action: Complete Table 1. Document the instrument choice for the tablets, the Tecator exclusions and the diesel sample structure.

issues.title: Practical usability: unlabelled-set size, prior availability, software
issues.description: The method needs unlabelled spectra to estimate the eigen-spectrum, but the paper does not report how many are needed or how sensitive the forecast is to a small or unrepresentative unlabelled set (Table S25 covers RPM-T only). A lab needs a default prior, i.e. r and logit-η location and scale by spectral region, sample type and preprocessing, and an easy implementation. The code is promised 'upon acceptance'.
issues.evidence: Sec. 2.5; Table S25; Data availability statement.
issues.corrective_action: Add a sensitivity curve for the number of unlabelled spectra (e.g. 50, 100, 300, all). Publish a table of default priors by family, spectral region and preprocessing. Provide a minimal function or worked notebook, and deposit the code for review now.
issues.proposed_experiment: For 6 tasks, subsample the unlabelled pool to 50/100/300/1000 spectra and report the change in B-RPM error and bias.

recommendation_rationale: The theoretical contribution (observability limit, identification set) is sound and relevant to chemometric practice. However, the paper presents itself as a planning tool, and its decision value is not demonstrated: no Brier gain, the identification set is almost always uninformative, the staged design is untested, and B-RPM is absent from the n-for-target analysis. The 'least biased' headline does not survive per-task analysis, and the abstract emphasises secondary endpoints while the pre-specified hypotheses failed. The required work is mostly computational on existing data: a staged-design simulation, PLS truth, reference-error-informed η, an expanded robustness study, and Riley/ASTM baselines. Together with rewritten claims and a shorter, more accessible theory section, this could make the paper suitable for ACA. If decision value still cannot be shown, the paper should be reframed as a diagnostic or negative-result contribution with correspondingly modest claims.
